label: Open flames and house fires
summary: Candles, oil lamps, kerosene heaters, wood stoves and camp stoves bring open flame indoors, often during power outages. A flame left with nobody watching, something that burns set too close, or a lamp or heater refuelled hot can start a house fire. For fumes, see Carbon monoxide.
signs: Candles in bedrooms, bathrooms or anywhere people may fall asleep, or closer than 30 cm (12 in) to anything that burns
A kerosene heater closer than about 1 m (3 ft) to furniture or clothing, or running without its protective grille
An Aladdin-type mantle lamp with anything that burns within 45 cm (18 in) around it or 90 cm (36 in) above the chimney (the maker’s figures)
A lamp flame that climbs or flickers, or flames coming out of the top of the chimney: an over-fired lamp can run away very quickly
Kerosene kept in a red can or one that once held petrol: it may be the wrong fuel or contaminated
No working smoke alarm, or alarms with dead or missing batteries
do: Use flashlights or other battery lights instead of candles where you can
Put candles in stable holders where they can't be knocked over, at least 30 cm (12 in) from anything that burns
Keep kerosene heaters at least 1 m (3 ft) from furniture and clothing; run them with the room door open, or a window open about 2.5 cm (1 in) if the room is closed off or the house is tight
Turn lamps and heaters off and let them cool before refuelling; fill heaters outdoors, never above the full mark, with clear 1-K kerosene, and lamps only with the fuel their maker names
Stand by any pan on a flame, and keep a pan lid or baking sheet nearby to cover a pan that catches fire; turn the burner off if it smokes or the grease boils
Keep battery smoke alarms on every level, outside sleeping areas and in bedrooms, and test them monthly
Fight a fire only while it is small and hasn't spread beyond where it started, standing between it and your way out: pull the pin, aim, squeeze and sweep. Otherwise get everyone out
dont: Don't leave a candle, lamp or burner lit when you leave the room or go to sleep
Don't put water on burning cooking oil or fuel: it spreads the fire. Smother a burning pan with its lid
Don't put petrol in a kerosene heater or lamp: even a little mixed in greatly raises the risk of fire or explosion
Don't move or carry a heater that flares up: switch it off if it has a shut-off, and get out if that doesn't stop it
Don't heat a room with a gas stove, or use barbecues, camp stoves or portable burners indoors or in a garage or basement: see Carbon monoxide
ppe: Cotton rather than synthetics near flames: nylon, polyester, acetate and polypropylene melt and stick to skin, even in blends
Leather gloves for stove doors, lamp chimneys and hot pots
Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms with battery backup
firstAid: Clothes on fire: don't run. Cover your face with your hands, drop to the ground and roll over and over until the flames are out
Someone else on fire: douse them with water or smother the flames with a fire blanket or other non-flammable material
Then cool burns under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20; take clothing and jewellery off the burned area, but leave anything stuck to the skin

Cover loosely with cling film (not on the face) or a clean cloth, with no ice, creams or oil. Burns wider than about 5–8 cm (2–3 in), burns on the face, hands, feet, joints or groin, and burns on a child need medical care
Anyone who breathed smoke: get them into fresh air and watch them as on the Carbon monoxide card; burns that make breathing hard need medical help at once
